subtopic: NATO-PROPOSED PLACING OF NUCLEAR MINES ON TURKISH BORDER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: NATO-PROPOSED PLACING OF NUCLEAR MINES ON TURKISH BORDER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Prime Minister is in a position to answer the question asked two days ago by my colleague the hon. member for York South. Perhaps I might be permitted to summarize the question. What attitude did the Minister of National Defence take toward the proposal made at the meeting of the nuclear planning group of NATO at Ankara? The proposal called for nuclear mines to be laid on the eastern border of Turkey which is also the border of the Soviet union. Can we be assured that Canada will oppose this proposal in view of our support of the principle of non-proliferation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: NATO-PROPOSED PLACING OF NUCLEAR MINES ON TURKISH BORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the nuclear planning group of NATO was established last year in order to permit the allies of the United States to participate in the formation of nuclear strategy. As my hon. friend knows, the ministers of defence of the member countries met at Ankara to consider the progress of a number of studies presently under way. One of those is on the question of atomic demolition mines. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the nuclear planning group is not a decision making body but, rather, makes recommendations to the NATO council.


The question of the use of atomic demolition mines as defensive weapons has been under consideration in NATO for some time. Because of the geographic situation of Turkey and the nature of the terrain of the Turko-Soviet border the Turkish government has been particularly interested in the possibility of using atomic demolition mines for the purpose of creating obstacles in the way of invading forces.
The nuclear planning group has accordingly been studying this question. Further study is being given to the matter, and the results are to be considered by the next ministerial meeting of the nuclear planning group in the spring of 1968. The Canadian position in connection with this proposal is primarily to assure ourselves that no arrangements would be recommended regarding these defensive weapons which could increase the danger of escalation or involve any form of nuclear proliferation.

subtopic: NATO-PROPOSED PLACING OF NUCLEAR MINES ON TURKISH BORDER
speechtext: Why is it, then, that in 1965 the Canadian government denied any knowledge of this matter and later, when it was brought out, decided that it was classified information?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NATO-PROPOSED PLACING OF NUCLEAR MINES ON TURKISH BORDER
speechtext: Order. The question is argumentative.

subtopic: NATO-PROPOSED PLACING OF NUCLEAR MINES ON TURKISH BORDER
speechtext: Then I will ask the Prime Minister a straightforward question. When did this information become unclassified?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the adjournment last evening I was directing my remarks to the Minister of Finance and I stated that the mere fact he has made two speeches in the last two days with regard to the economic state of the nation clearly indicates the seriousness of the situation and the inability of the government and more particularly his own inability to cope with the problems and to provide adequate solutions. When one thinks of the Minister of Finance one thinks of a person who has attempted to show the Canadian
[Mr. Hees.l
DEBATES	October 5, 1967
people how to manage their own affairs, to show how he would balance the deficits of the nation, and how, by practising frugality and good management, we would have prosperity and stability.
I pointed out to him that this has not been so since he has taken office and I set forth three examples to prove how miserably he has failed to come to grips with these problems. The first example was the consumer price index which has shown a steady increase in the Canadian economy. I indicated to him that the Dominion Bureau of Statistics' figures show that the consumer price index has increased from 139.5 in July, 1965 to 144.3 in July, 1966 and to 150.2 in July, 1967. This would indicate that the Canadian people are paying, as of July of this year, $150.20 for purchases for which they would have paid $100 in 1949. I also told the minister that in my opinion the people whom this situation affects most are those who live on fixed incomes such as the old age pensioners and people in the lower income bracket.
The second problem with which the minister has failed to deal is unemployment. Unemployment has been a continuing festering sore on the Canadian economy. D.B.S. figures inform us that since 1965 there has been an upward trend in unemployment despite occasional seasonal declines. In July, 1967, the number of unemployed stood at 330,000 in absolute figures. Shown as a percentage of the labour force, the number of unemployed has increased steadily since the end of 1965 despite periodic declines. I said that graphs published by D.B.S. indicate a steady increase in unemployment since the beginning of 1966. In fact the D.B.S. table, which is adjusted to seasonal variations, indicates that in Ontario the number of unemployed is 3.5 per cent. In the Atlantic provinces the number has increased to 6.8 per cent, and even in the province of British Columbia the figure stands at 5 per cent. This is a disgrace to the Canadian economy.
The third point I mentioned concerns the high interest rates which were reflected in the recent increase in the N.H.A. rate on mortgages to 8.25 per cent. I indicated to the minister that in areas such as Toronto interest rates vary from 8.75 to 9 per cent. At that point the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) challenged the figure of 9 per cent and suggested that in Toronto interest rates for conventional loans only varied .5 per cent. I should like the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour to know that according to the information I have received the rate on
October 5, 1967

loans on prime properties in Toronto stands at 8.5 per cent and on secondary properties the variation is between .25 and .5 per cent, which would bring it close to 9 per cent. The interest rate on prime properties in Sudbury stands at 9 per cent and the interest rate on prime properties in London, Ontario is 8.75 per cent.
I also pointed out that the guaranteed investment certificates of the National Trust Company now pay 6.75 per cent and that in order for the company to make a margin of profit it would have to lend money at a rate of interest between 8.5 and 9 per cent. These were three of the items that I mentioned in the house last evening.
Yesterday we heard the remedies which the Minister of Finance proposed to some of these problems. He stated that the real causes could not be found in any one place and he suggested there may be two areas in which the government and business can show restraint. The first one was restraint on government expenditures, and he indicated that the government has made special efforts to trim down the estimates for the next year and that it will be his aim to reduce our present deficit.
The cutting back of government expenditures has also been proposed by the Conservative party. In fact the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) yesterday took the government to task with regard to government expenditures without making suggestions as to what expenditures the government should reduced with the exception of the social and welfare areas. He said in fact that if we cannot afford to pay for old age pensions and medicare programs we should make cut-backs in those areas. This appears to be a far cry from the pressure which the Progressive Conservative party tried to apply during the early part of the year to increase old age pensions for the senior citizens of the country. The Conservative party has not indicated, nor has the Minister of Finance, that in cutting back government expenditures we should cut subsidies to the wheat farmers or cut our defence budget thereby affecting the maritime provinces and the province of British Columbia. The members of that party have not suggested that we cut the subsidies to the coal industry and no suggestion has been made with regard to a cut-back on educational grants or other social services.
It is true that government expenditures have risen within the last few years but it has been to cover an increase in social and
The Budget-Mr. Gilbert welfare programs, educational grants, transportation, interest on the public debt and subsidies. All these increases have been necessary for the over-all good of the country and they are to be expected. The Economic Council of Canada stated that in the future the government must participate in these types of programs if the progress and prosperity of the Canadian people are to continue. All too often increases in government expenditures are translated into a criticism of increasing government waste in its departments and agencies and of the application of Parkinson's law as well as excessive bureaucracy and lax administrative control. It is necessary that the government adopt better measures of reviewing and auditing government expenses, but this is secondary to its main function of determining the priorities of the government in facilitating high standards of performance in the nation's economic and social development, for example, with regard to education, health and welfare, transportation, resources development and the improvement of the quality of life of all Canadians.
a (3:30 p.m.)
We in the New Democratic party feel that the government has failed miserably in determining the priorities for its expenditures. The most flagrant example is this regard in the field of housing. The serious shortage of housing today is an indication of the lack of foresight and leadership of the federal government in respect of an urgent and pressing problem.
The solution of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) appears in Hansard for Monday, October 2, where as reported at page 2730 he recognized the problem and stated:
-there is no doubt that now there is a shortage of housing accommodation in Canada. This shortage, of course, is particularly to be found in the very rapidly growing urban centres, one of which I help to represent in this House.
The minister then set forth his solution to the housing problem in Canada and as reported at page 2731 said:
The first problem we have to deal with, if we are going to face up to the housing problem adequately and not in a partisan fashion, looking at the realities of the situation, is the shortage of capital or I might say, if you want to put it another way, the shortage of savings.
Then the minister went on to set forth the necessity for high interest rates to attract United States capital to participate in the economy; otherwise there would be a drop in the housing program. The minister said:
Canadian rates must be high enough in relation to those of the United States that they will attract
October 5, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Gilbert
into Canada the capital required to supply our deficiency. This is just a fact of life. There is nothing we can do about it unless we can increase our own savings-
That is his solution to the housing problem, Mr. Speaker. I was hoping that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) would be in the house because I wanted to remind him that in the symposium on housing held in Toronto in the spring of this year the former president of Central Mortgage and Housing, Mr. Mansur, took an entirely different approach to this problem. The minister has stated that there is a shortage of savings. Mr. Mansur stated that the real problem with housing in Canada today is not a shortage of mortgage funds but the high cost of houses. The main elements in the high cost of houses are the high cost of land, the high cost of labour and materials, and the high cost of interest rates. In fact, Mr. Mansur put it rather dramatically and said that there was enough mortgage money pouring out of the ears of the finance companies to take care of this problem but it was just that we have outpriced ourselves because of the high cost of housing.
This is a far different approach from that taken by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance who say there is a shortage of savings and that we do not have the necessary capital. We in the New Democratic party say that there is a shortage of savings by the Canadian people, that it is the lack of direction and the misallocation of funds to meet the present economic and social needs of the country that is the cause.
I should like to give hon. members an example. Many people say that Canadians are great savers. There is plenty of evidence to support this contention. In 1947 Canadian savings amounted to $6 billion, in 1950 to $7 billion, in 1955 to $10 billion, in 1960 to $15 billion, in 1965 to $25 billion and 1966 to $27 billion. This indicates the tremendous savings that are made by the Canadian people.
The problem as we see it is the direction of the savings of the Canadian people. The main bodies that control the savings of the Canadian people are the lending institutions. For example, I should like to mention the direction of Canadian investments by the Canadian life insurance companies. In Canada life insurance companies do about 50 per cent of the insurance business; the balance is in the hands of United States and English companies. According to the superintendent of insurance, total investment in 1965 on the part of Canadian insurance companies amounted to $12 billion. These investments


comprised four main	categories-bonds,
stocks, mortgage loans and other assets. The report of the superintendent indicates that only 65 per cent of this $12 billion was invested in Canada. The remaining 35 per cent was invested in the United States, the commonwealth and other countries. We feel that there should be a high percentage of the savings of Canadians directed to investment in Canada so as to take care of the economic and social needs of the nation.
Although one is disappointed at the investment picture of the insurance companies, one can be greatly disturbed when one looks at the mutual funds in Canada. They have no social conscience whatsoever. In fact, most of the investments of the mutual funds are not placed in Canada. The great majority of these funds, the savings of the Canadian people, are invested in the United States. Therefore we feel that the government must give direction to the savings of Canadians so as to provide the necessary money for the development of Canada. There would not be this serious housing crisis today if the government had given direction to the lending institutions in investing the savings of the Canadian people.
Another area where Canadian savers could place their money is in the Canada Development Corporation, which could be another useful instrument in the development of Canada by providing an opportunity for Canadians to participate in the development of the country and giving them a fair return on their money. However, Mr. Speaker, the government has been talking about this corporation for quite some time but as yet has not taken any action. One is therefore led to believe that the main reason the government has not taken action is that the very institutions that give money to the government at election time have either discouraged or restrained the government from doing so. We as Canadians cannot buy back Canadian industry, as has been stated by one of the ministers of the government. We must direct the investments of Canadians to the development of industry and to meeting the social needs of the country.
Another area where the government could show leadership is in resource industries such as mining, oil, pulp and paper and the like. Here the government should be giving direction and encouragement to develop our manufacturing industries in Canada and help them specialize so they can supply the home market as well as compete successfully in the international market. Too many of our
October 5, 1967

natural resources are being exported to countries like the United States, where in turn manufacturers make the products which we in Canada have to buy back again. We feel that greater emphasis should be placed on our natural resources and more opportunity given to Canadian companies to develop these resources to their full utility so they can make products we now have to buy from our neighbour to the south and are also able to compete successfully in the international market.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Perhaps the best example of this is to be seen in the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) as they appear in the minutes of the meeting of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs of June 13. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) asked the minister the following question having to do with the production of nickel in Canada. On page 57 of the report the following appears:
I would like to ask the minister to make some further comments on a matter that he discussed in the house on June 5 with my colleague, Mr. Saltsman, on the question of the nickel production and supplies of nickel for the domestic market.
I have here a report in the Globe and Mail of April 20 of the annual meeting of the International Nickel Company, and this does not seem to track very well with the reports of D.B.S. and with your own statement, Mr. Minister, about the production of nickel. Mr. Wingate had this to say:
"Production this year will be a record but not as great as last year's deliveries of 500.2 million pounds, which included 100 million pounds of U.S. government surplus nickel sold at no profit."
I was wondering if I could get some explanation of what that means.
I have also had reports of domestic users who have been restricted in their deliveries while at the same time our exports to the United States have been increasing. The fact is reported that in 1966 we exported 1.7 million pounds more than we produced.
I was wondering if the government has in mind any possibility of stockpiling a certain amount of it here in Canada rather than leaving some of our domestic users in short supply and continuing the exports to the United States at the rate they are presently being undertaken.
The minister replied:
The stockpile in the United States has distorted the supply and demand figures. There has been a drawdown on the stockpile which gave the impression that there was a greater availability of nickel than there really is from world production. World production is not able to meet world demand at the present time, and the stockpile is getting pretty well eroded. The strike at Sudbury last year distorted the production figures considerably and set back the supply side of the supply and demand relationship.
The Budget-Mr. Gilbert
International Nickel has been pressed to meet demands on a world basis for nickel; they have not been able to cope with it. In this situation, they have undertaken to provide to Canadian users-
This is the important sentence:
-100 per cent of their utilization of last year.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands then said:
But with no provision for any expansion in their operations.
Later he said:
Does the government not think that the primary objective of the government should be to see to the expansion of Canadian industry that is dependent on nickel supplies?
The minister replied:
We think that is a primary objective; but, as I said, we have got to balance that against our export commitments, and we attach great Importance in Canada to a high level of exports.
That shows that the government puts great stress on export of our natural resources. I think the evidence is obvious, as we see it, that the government will give to Canadian industry only 100 per cent of the utilization of 1966, with no provision for expansion. We say that Canadian natural resources should be made available first to Canadian manufacturers. Canadian industry should be developed first and only the surplus ought to be exported.
The N.D.P. also feels that an investment advisory board ought to be set up to guide the investment of retained earnings of Canadian corporations within the country. Such a measure would cope with many economic and social problems. The Minister of Finance is quite familiar with the technique involved. Not long ago he imposed a 5 per cent surcharge tax on Canadian corporations. He allowed them 5 per cent on their money and promised to return it with interest within a period not to exceed 36 months. The minister became generous and returned their money to the corporations within a much shorter period. Now the minister talks of an excess of demand in the Canadian economy. Perhaps he ought to impose a similar tax again, but this time he might be well advised to lead our corporations toward the best types of investment to keep our economy stable and growing.
To dampen inflationary tendencies the minister said yesterday that he would ask industry and labour to restrain themselves with regard to prices and wages. I submit it is only fair, if labour unions in Canada are to

October 5. 1967
The Budget-Mr. Davis go through the complex process of negotiation, mediation, conciliation and arbitration before going on strike for higher wages, that Canadian corporations ought to be placed in a similar position. That is why for some time we have urged the government to set up a prices review board. It would examine any unjustifiable increases in the prices of Canadian goods. As the government imposes the restrictions I have mentioned on labour, surely it has a duty to impose similar restrictions on industry. Just asking industry to restrain its pricing policy while at the same time proposing a complex process for the trade unions to follow is not fair in the circumstances.
Substantially, Canadians must run their own economy for their own development; they should not be the tools of corporations when it comes to direction and development. This party feels that if we were to implement the measures I have tried to outline Canada would enjoy more stable growth and our people would become the first priority.

There are several other figures to which I want to direct the attention of the house. There is, first of all, the order of magnitude of the transfers to the provinces. I said we were running a deficit of 2 per cent on a national accounts basis. We have a total budget on that basis of the order of $11 billion. Of that amount, $2 billion goes to the provinces as a direct transfer into provincial treasuries. Thus, if hon. members want a true picture of what the federal government spends for federal purposes within the B.N.A. Act, it can be said we were running a surplus of nearly 20 per cent. The federal government has certainly balanced its budget. It is handing over to the provinces no less than $2 billion and the provinces are using this money for local and provincial economies.
It is not easy to produce figures showing the extent of federal assistance province by province, but one can get some indication of them from the reports of the Economic Council of Canada. Reading the second report of the council I find that in Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island at least 50 per cent of the provinces income is derived from Ottawa in one form or another-equalization payments, payments in connection with joint cost programs, and so on. In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick federal assistance ranges between 30 per cent and 40 per cent. In Quebec, Manitoba and Saskatchewan it is about 20 per cent and even in the so-called "have" provinces, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, federal support for all provincial purposes, including municipal purposes, amounts to about 15 per cent.
Thus, when we look at the federal budget we are looking at more than the national accounts as they relate to moneys taken in and expended for purely national purposes. We are looking also at surpluses generated for payment to the provinces, not only to those with low average income and high unemployment but to all of them.
We have certainly introduced a number of expensive programs in the area of social security. However, I should like to point out that most of these are not in themselves inflationary. We have made new expenditures and in some cases we have obliged the provinces to incur new expenditures. But we have always made sure that the revenue necessary to meet these payments is available. The programs have been organized in that fashion.
The Budget-Mr. Davis
Consider, for example, the old age assistance legislation. I well remember how bitterly both the official opposition and the New Democratic party criticized the increase in taxation which the Minister of Finance introduced to meet the cost of increases in these pensions. But as a result of the action he took the whole of the old age pension account is now in balance. As much is being taken out of the economy as is necessary to make these benefits available to our older citizens. The old age program, as it has been managed by the minister, is not inflationary.
The Canada Pension Plan is not inflationary. There were many who said that more would be taken from the Canadian people in the form of contributions than would ever flow back into the economy through reinvestment by provincial governments. Ottawa has been the keeper of the accounts; it has been collecting this money and passing it on to the provincial governments. The plan has not been inflationary and the money paid out has not exceeded income contrary to the dour expectation of pessimists opposite. It has not had a depressing effect on our economy; it has not, of itself, been inflationary.
The unemployment insurance fund is in the black. It was in the red back in 1961 and 1962. Today it is managed in such a way as to be substantially in balance. Even the government legislation having to do with medicare contains its own provision for balancing income and expenditure. If people take a sufficiently broad view of the medicare scheme they must realize that there will be few, if any, more doctors at work after the plan is introduced than there are at the present time. The doctors will not suddenly be submitting larger bills and charging higher fees to their patients. In other words, a different system of accounting will be in effect. The manner of collection and payment will have been changed but the economic impact of keeping our accounts in a different way will not be appreciable. Indeed, I have sufficient faith in the medical profession to think that medicare will not be inflationary at all and that we will be getting good value for our money under a financial scheme which sees a mixture of public and private plans in effect across the nation. These new arrangements in themselves are not inflationary.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
What can be controlled and certainly influenced by the actions of the government

October 5, 196?
The Budget-Mr. Davis are the expenditures of many of our departments. Here the most inflationary single element is in the category of salaries and wages. For example, take the accounts of the Department of National Defence. I remember the former minister, now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), explaining his estimates last June. He made it abundantly clear that if it had not been for salary and wage increases, increases in pay and allowances to the armed forces, his budget would have been down by about 10 per cent. The very modest increase in the national defence budget is entirely due to increased wages, salaries, pay and allowances.
This problem of increased wages and salaries runs throughout the entire civil service and throughout the economy in general, but certainly that the area of the civil service, of the departments, is one that should be under the control of the government and the government should do something about it. I think the sort of thing the government should do is to go slow on its hirings. On balance let retirements reduce the payroll of many of our departments. I know of a few examples where branches, boards and departments have increased not twice or three times in the last decade but have gone up 10 or 15 times through proliferation, through the rounding out of jobs which do not need to be done in such an elaborate fashion. I would like to be quite specific in respect of some of our crown corporations.
I notice according to the estimates in the blue book that for the current year C.B.C. expenditure is to go up by some $30 million, from $115 million to approximately $145 million. I do not think there is anyone in this country who is not alarmed about the budget of the C.B.C., but there are very few people who seem to be able to put their fingers on some of the difficulties, the errors, the miscalculations, the plain mismanagement that goes on within that large corporation. It badly needs a shaking up, and I am sure it will get a shaking up as soon as the new broadcasting act has been introduced and a new management installed.
To give an example, I have a clipping here from the Vancouver Sun of September 29, 1967. It is a column written by Mr. Les Wedman. In it he refers to a so-called popular program which has appeared on C.T.V., "Mission Impossible," a United States produced series. C.T.V. ran the series last year for a given fee. However, before C.T.V. could reach the source of the series in the United States to cancel it for the coming year, they

were met by a shamefaced executive from the company which films "Mission Impossible" who said that C.T.V. could not have it anyway because they had been outbid. The C.B.C. is going to run it this year for twice the price. The C.B.C. had not even bothered to check with C.T.V. to see whether it could take up C.T.V.'s option and get the series for half the price that we, the Canadian taxpayers, are now going to pay for that program.
I think some hon. members opposite will be interested in another example given in Mr. Wedman's column, dealing with the coverage of the recent Progressive Conservative convention at the Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto. Certainly the television coverage was good, and everyone I have talked to thought it was a great event. I think it was a very fine event and deserved full coverage. I only trust that future conventions will get as good coverage but here is what Mr. Wedman wrote about it:
C.B.C. spent in excess of $400,000 to cover the convention and used 486 people to bring it to viewers. C.T.V.-with more hours on the air and scooping C.B.C. all along the line-did a better job with only 48 people at a cost of $43,000.
C.T.V. did the job for roughly one tenth the cost and with one tenth of the personnel used by C.B.C. Probably the C.B.C. could have held its own convention in Toronto at the same time and it would have been an impressive one with all those people present. But it is not good value for the taxpayers' money.

speechtext:
Later. Now we are going to have a federally financed crossing built over the harbour in Vancouver but the costs will be substantially, if not totally, repaid by tolls. The costs will be defrayed substantially if not totally by the users of the facility, with the federal government merely acting as a banker just as it does with respect to housing. This is fine. The user knows what he is getting and what he is paying for it.
In this connection I point out that the people of my riding, who number 150,000, look with some envy at the people of Prince Edward Island. The people of Prince Edward Island, whose population is 105,000 have been promised that a crossing will be built between the mainland and Prince Edward Island. It may well be a causeway. This is an obligation of the Canadian people that dates back to confederation. I think all of us agree that the people of Canada should shoulder the cost of a good, adequate, but economic means of transportation and communication between Prince Edward Island and the rest of the country. This is agreed, but I would like to be assured that we all get good value for our money.
I have seen various estimates of the cost of a causeway to Prince Edward Island varying from $100 million to $150 million and maybe more. I might point out that there are other ways of getting people and goods backward and forward across water. On Vancouver island we have 330,000 people, three times the population of Prince Edward Island. There are greater distances involved. Far greater tonnages of goods and numbers of people move across Georgia strait than between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, and we do this with a capital investment of less than $70 million. Approximately 5 million people moved backwards and forwards between the mainland and Vancouver island last year, well over 1 million vehicles, freight cars, goods of all kinds in bulk and in packages and all this, as I say, for a capital investment of less than $70 million.
I know that the federal government looks at alternatives quite seriously. If a mixture of public and private enterprise can do a job on the west coast of this order of magnitude for a capital investment of $70 million, then it should also take another look at the causeway proposal and the alternatives to it. In fact I expect the government to take a hard look at the alternatives. The government must see if a causeway will last almost indefinitely with little maintenance because in that case possibly the benefits would exceed the cost in the 27053-1801
The Budget-Mr. Davis
long run and so a causeway could still be the answer.
[DOT] (4:io p.m.)
I want to be sure, however, and know at first hand through seeing the arithmetic, that the right decision is being made. I do not wish this just for myself. I want the people of my riding and the people on the west coast to know this. One of the things they grumble about is investment of this nature where they believe the federal government is engaging in give-away programs merely to buy votes. Obviously, from the result of the last federal election, causeways do not buy any seats in the House of Commons, although they may-still be important in the eyes of some people.
Then there is the matter of the coal subsidies. Much has been made of this. I am glad to see that in the blue book they are down by about $3 million in the estimates for this fiscal year. This is a move in the right direction. I do not like subsidies. I want to see the subsidies used in the movement of coal from western sources in the prairies and British Columbia to the coast eliminated. All this coal is moving to Japan for the steel and power industries there.
I do not believe we should be subsidizing exports in this way, especially exports of a non-renewable resource. I have been told that the Japanese do not want coal on the basis that there is substantial government support because the government in the country of origin might pull its subsidy out some day and they would be caught with a bill which they would have to pay for many years after. I think that in order to trade with the Japanese in respect of coal we should do it on a businesslike basis without subsidy, as private enterprise would do it.
I gather that one of the terms of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and one of the understandings among nations in respect of the promotion of more trade throughout the world is that countries should not subsidize their exports in this way. This is one area in which Canada really has not been living up to the principles of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. I believe it is good policy to phase out the subsidies on coal for export which moves from our western coal mines. As a member from the west I think I can speak for many western people on this subject. I know that the great majority of the people in my part of the world would be glad to see these subsidies phased out. Here is another place where

October 5, 1967
The Budget-r-Mr. Davis the government can save some money and be businesslike as well.
I should like to refer now to the matter of atomic energy and research. In 1961 I had the temerity to appear before a committee of this house on research. I suggested that benefit cost studies be carried out on a nuclear power program in this country. I suggested that one of the questions which should be answered is what should be the appropriate level of research in the broad area of nuclear power production. At that time I suggested that the $40 million budget be cut back and that some of the cut-back might be used in other areas of research. I could be wrong. But I would still like to see a benefit cost analysis done on our present program in an effort to see whether the benefits exceed the cost, allowing always that there is some uncertainty about whether our reactors will be the best in the world and whether nuclear energy will in fact be cheaper than certain other alternative sources of power.
The budget of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is in the order of $70 million this year. Thus far we have spent about half a billion dollars on nuclear research and development in respect of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and its related activities in this country. Half a billion dollars is a lot of money. It could go a long way toward buying many alternative benefits and paying for other research. I am not saying the money is misspent. We have a first class reactor and possibly a world leader; I hope it is, but this has yet to be proven.
Must we continually go on pumping money into research in this country at the rate of $70 million a year? It is interesting to note that the United Kingdom finally has decided not to keep in the running in the area of jet aircraft development. This program became quite expensive. They did not drop out as dramatically as we did in respect of the Arrow program, but they found they could not compete with the subsidized jet program of the United States. Now the United Kingdom is wondering whether it should do the same thing in respect of atomic energy.
Why should we not do a good cost benefit analysis in respect of the atomic energy program in this country so that we can either be comforted in the knowledge that we are spending money on the right scale or be informed concerning the right order of magnitude of any cut-back? Although I was a scientist at one time, I am not one of those who believe that a scientist is any different from anybody else. He likes to run his own

empire and have more people working for him. He is no different from anyone else; he is dedicated and wants to do a good job. But he lacks perspective and he is the last person to ask how much money should be spent on his program in the public interest.
The Science Council of Canada recently made a recommendation, or at least a meaningful reference, to a project called I.N.G., the intense neutron generator project. It is rather fond of this project, as is Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. At page 12 of the first annual report of the Science Council of Canada, 1966-67, we find that these-
-research facilities would cost over $150 million to build, spread over a seven-year construction period, and that the operating budget in succeeding years would be over $20 million per annum.
This might be fine but we would be putting a lot of eggs in a single basket. I would rather see ten separate projects costing $15 million and ten separate projects with operating charges of $2 million a year paid out of the federal treasury in respect of experiments related more closely to the processing of our resources. This alternative of carrying out different researches with different research teams, different research leaders and so on, a variety of programs rather than one big one or a very few big ones, I think is sound. Certainly it spreads the risk. I believe it is economically defensible and fits in better with the regional development of this country in that we would have research scattered regionally across Canada and not situated in one spot at the centre of our great nation.
In respect of social security, I think our social security program is excellent. I believe a great many measures have been brought in in respect of which we can all take pride. These are measures which Canadians are gradually coming to understand. But for the time being at least we have gone far enough with expensive programs. I was therefore glad that the Prime Minister said in an interview with Mr. Ross of the press gallery, as reported in the July edition of Maclean's:
-we've pretty well established what I have called the basic foundation of social security. From now on, we will improve and refine rather than extend.
Personally I was very much heartened by that comment, as I am sure many other people were as well.

speechtext:
October 5, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Davis process we will improve our productivity. The Economic Council of Canada has been harping on the question of productivity, and well it might. We need to improve our output per man-hour. We can do this if people move to areas of greater opportunity, to growth areas with new industries. In these areas the latent abilities of people could really be put to work.
There are many initiatives which I should like to see the federal government take in the months and years ahead. I should like to see us not only set up a department of urban affairs or a department of housing and urban affairs, or whatever the title may be, but one which would deal with more than just being the banker for people who need housing. I should like to see the federal government enter even more into the planning process with the municipalities.
I should like to see such a department help to solve not just the housing problems of people but their transportation problems, their sewage disposal problems, and so on. I should like to see the department deal with the provision of services primarily through its banking function. In effect, the money would be lent and it would be paid back by the users. It would be directly related to the value received. I think this is the businesslike way of doing things and I should like to see the federal government act more in this way.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the National Housing Act of this country have been great successes. These were federal initiatives in an area which the constitutional lawyer has always said was reserved to the provinces. Ottawa took the lead in the early 1940's. It established a building code. Many progressive municipalities adopted the code. Progressive municipalities, provincial governments and private organizations have joined in creating facilities which would not otherwise have existed. Shelter has been provided for people of different incomes and in all parts of the country. This has been all to the good.
In respect of transportation I should like to see the federal government do what has been done by the federal government of the United States. That government has built great highways, throughways, connecting streets and so on through a special fund. This fund has been developed by imposing a tax of roughly one cent per gallon on gasoline and diesel oil. The tax money accumulating in the fund is paid out to municipalities in order that they may build highways, throughways, connecting streets, etc. The federal authorities in the

United States make sure that there is adequate planning and they often help the municipalities to plan. Once the plans are agreed upon the federal government of the United States, through this fund, puts up as much as 90 per cent of the capital cost of all the new facilities they need.
We could at least go 50-50 with the municipalities, or the municipalities and/or the provincial governments. The user of these facilities the man paying the one cent a gallon tax, would be seeing the results of the tax turning up in terms of more efficient streets, better highways and less time lost in transit. I am sure he would get value for the money paid in the form of this tax. He would get value in the form of a lessening of the time taken to travel, reduction of the wear on tires, brake shoes, and so on. I am sure he would see a reasonable relationship between this tax and the facilities progressively made available to him. He would also see an account that would be in balance.
In putting such a program into effect we would be relating benefits much more directly to costs. This is the type of program that we need. We need it, by all means, with the help and blessing of the provinces, but I for one would not drag my feet and wait indefinitely for all the provinces to get on this bandwagon because, as the Economic Council of Canada has so clearly pointed out, the urban problem, the great movement of Canadians from outlying areas into our big cities, is going to be with us a long time.
We are reaching the point where 80 per cent of our people will be living in the great metropolitan areas. The figure will perhaps be 85 per cent by the turn of the century. So let us have a department that looks ahead in trying to solve the biggest single problem that we face. Let us have not just departments dealing with rural affairs and matters like ARDA and so on, praiseworthy as they may be, but a department that deals more with the really big problems of the future, problems that will involve many more people who will have even greater difficulties adjusting themselves to the circumstances in which they find themselves.

speechtext:
I am just coming to the end of my remarks, Mr. Speaker. We need to tie benefits to costs. We need a more meaningful accounting of our economy. I also believe that we need-I know this is not the opinion of the government and it does not appear to
October 5, 1967	COMMONS
be the opinion of the Economic Council of Canada-guide lines in instituting such a program. I do not mean rigid guide lines laid out in legislation but the frequent reiteration of what is reasonable in respect of wages, what is reasonable in respect of price increases.
I believe in a modest degree of inflation, not inflation that continues indefinitely but perhaps 1 per cent or 2 per cent a year, in order to keep the economy buoyant and growing.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
But I do not believe in inflation that is up in the 5 to 10 per cent bracket. An inflation of 1 per cent per year, accompanied by a 2 per cent per annum increase in productivity, will tolerate an average wage increase of 3 per cent a year or at the most 4 per cent a year. Our economy cannot tolerate wage increases or price increases of more than 3 to 4 per cent a year on the average without genuinely affecting those who rely on their savings or those on fixed incomes who are bound to be hurt by inflation in any case but are badly hurt by inflation that is running away.
The main message I am trying to get across is the need for a better accounting of our income and our expenses. I would more closely relate revenues to expenditures. I would do this on a program basis. I would want to be sure that benefits exceed costs and that we are going to engage in programs which have the highest relation of benefits to costs, not just more benefits than costs but a benefit to cost ratio of two or three to one. There are many opportunities in this country which will turn out to have benefit to cost ratios of that order of magnitude. We need to grasp them and we need to be more businesslike.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance say that he is cutting back, that he is determined to have a balanced budget, at least balanced on a national accounts basis, next year. We are growing very rapidly. Our economy has a high head of steam on but it needs at least a balanced budget, not a deficit budget, in national accounts terms if we are not to add to the fires of inflation.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I also apologize to the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac for making him listen to me.
Some remarks have already been made in the house in a more formal way with regard to the changes in the ministry. I was not present at the time and I do not intend to say anything on this subject although normally I would. The only suggestion I have to make along these lines, which I hope will be passed on to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), is that when further changes are made I hope they will involve the shifting sideways of some of the present ornaments of the cabinet benches. Never have I seen so many gloomy and dejected faces peering at us, even with the problems posed by the lighting system here, as we have seen inhabiting the treasury benches in the last week or ten days. I do not resent their gloom. Never has a group of men worked so hard and toiled so diligently and so brilliantly to earn the right to be gloomy, and I give them this privilege. They are entitled to it, but it would be nice if they shifted sideways a little once in a while.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), in his second contribution to the budget debate, indicated certain views with
October 5, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin regard to the position of the economy and the position of the government. In one instance he referred to the great attempts being made by the government to curtail expenditures in the estimates for the coming year. My good friend, the learned and hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), has already dealt with this subject. I want to make another reference to it at this time because I think it is very important. I agree entirely with what the hon. member for Edmonton West said but I think there is more to the matter. The Minister of Finance would have us believe that a great melodrama takes place at the meetings of the Treasury Board, that, like Horatio at the bridge, the minister lays about lustily with his broad, red pencil, mutilating and destroying various estimates from time to time, and that the floor of the Treasury Board room is littered with the corpses of these projects. I wonder whether this is so. It seems to me more likely that something entirely different takes place, and I might give my view of it very briefly.
Let us say the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) is discussing her estimates. The Minister of Finance would say: "Judy, I see $1 billion for the new five year project of the C.B.C., for the anticipated five year program. You know our new rules and regulations concerning economy. I think we have to cut you down somewhere. I see one item of $25.67 in your estimate of $1 billion for whisk brooms to brush dust off the clothes of the dignified commentators and their guests on the program "Twenty Million Questions". I think we should cut out this $25.67 and when that has been done we can say you have conformed to the new regulations."
Let us say that in another instance the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) is asking for $900 million for medicare and other welfare programs for the next year. An item might be included there with respect to which the Minister of Finance might say: "Allan, I see an item for $5,400 covering the services of a filing clerk to file newspaper clippings of speeches made by your fellow Nova Scotian who has recently arrived in Ottawa. Having in mind that we may not need to employ this filing clerk at full capacity, possibly we could dispense with this item of $5,400."
I believe this is the kind of discussion which takes place at a meeting of the Treasury Board, but we are ready to wait and see. I suggest that the minister and the government make every possible effort to

bring down these estimates as soon as possible and let the standing committees examine and compare them with the programs of previous years so as to see to what extent there has been a real effort to reduce expenditures to manageable proportions.
I must say I was a little worried by the statement of the Minister of Finance when he indicated yesterday that an attempt would be made only to reduce the growth in expenditures. I took a little time and went through the estimates of several of the departments. Four of the departments in which changes have taken place have dealt with comparable projects, namely, the Departments of Labour, Manpower and Immigration, Secretary of State and Citizenship. My calculation is, comparing the actual expenditures for the fiscal year 1962-63 with the actual expenditures for the fiscal year 1966-67, that there has been an increase of over $400 million.

speechtext:
I am not here at this stage to do anything else than deal with the efforts of the government and the budgetary proposals of the Minister of Finance and to see whether or not the government has justified the faith which the people of Canada put in it. It seems to me that it has not. The fact is that there has been an increase of $400 million in those years. I suggest that these are the kind of programs that the standing committees of the house, exercising their functions intelligently and responsibly, should examine so as to see to what extent there has been a real effort on the part of the government to reduce the programs, as has been suggested by the Minister of Finance.
Apart from that, Mr. Speaker, and getting to the heart of the issue here, this government stands charged that it has mismanaged both its affairs and the affairs of the country, particularly in the realm of the economy, and not only has not done the things it should have done but has done things it should not have done. If I could, Mr. Speaker, I would call as witnesses here to substantiate my allegation all of the people in the country who over the last year to year and a half have been trying diligently to secure for themselves adequate housing accommodation. I am not going to go into that question. We have had an interesting debate on it as well as one or two motions and some questions. I think these people alone, this long, dreary queue of pepple, who in their essential and reasonable
October 5, 1967

This is the sort of thing which every small businessman and farmer has to contend with. When a farmer harvests his grain, when a businessman looks at his year-end statement, he asks: How much money shall I put into a new house, how much shall I plow back into the business or farm? It is important for the government to think this way.
Taxes and appropriations do not create wealth; they redistribute it. The only way to create wealth is by the application of labour to natural resources. That is what the government ought to have looked at for a long time. We can point to the record of the previous government in projects such as roads to resources program. We can point to the imaginative proposal-vocational training schools-which was advanced by the hon. member who is now acting leader of this party and was then the minister of labour. We can also point to one of the brightest jewels in our party's diadem, our party's contribution to national development, the Pine Point Railway. It was brought about in the face of bitter obstruction from the then opposition which now forms the government. Projects such as these create wealth. This project created a great increase in national wealth at no real cost to people.
One fault which can be attributed to this government is its refusal to recognize and deal with this aspect of the use of our national income.

speechtext:
We have heard the minister already, Mr. Speaker. No doubt we shall hear from him again. The charge I have levelled at the government will hardly be met by extraneous observations of this kind.
I really enjoyed the words the minister used in his defence. He said that we must manage prosperity; earlier he had said that we must pace the economy. I delight in these words. As I recognize them, they amount to an admission by the government that we have a serious problem of inflation and we must try to do something about it. I go along with the minister on that score.
The minister's speech yesterday, in which he tried to defend his policies, reminded me of the surgeon who after an operation talks to his colleagues and says: "Yes, the operation was a tremendous success, it was highly technical, everything was fine, but the unfortunate patient died.'' That was the type of defence the minister offered us yesterday.

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
The government is flustered and annoyed by the criticisms. It counters by saying, "Well, what would you do if you were us" or "why did you vote for such and such a project?" That is not germane at this time. The government sought for and secured from the people of this country the power to govern. It must govern. The collective conduct of the government is always a legitimate issue because it involves the assessment to be made by the public as to the government's fitness to carry on governing. That fitness is to be decided at an election.
I know that the position is difficult. The options open to the government have now narrowed. Perhaps I might make one parting statement in this regard. The government's actions might be compared to those of the captain of a fishing schooner. As you will notice, Mr. Speaker, this party has taken on a somewhat more nautical aspect in the last few weeks. I am speaking of the captain of a fishing schooner who, in the face of radio warnings of storms, in the face of storm signals, nevertheless insists on taking his ship out to sea. When he is caught in a hurricane he whines, whimpers, wrings his hands and says: "What are we to do?" That is the position of the government today. Of course, the captain can lighten his vessel and trim his cargo. He may do a number of things.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I must say something about these things because I believe hon. members are very disturbed by the statement made by the minister yesterday, which appeared to constitute a warning that steps would be taken to increase taxation or otherwise to affect a cooling off in the economy. This holds out the spectre of artificially created unemployment as a means of relief from the difficulties in which we find ourselves. I reject such a proposal. While it is true that the Economic Council of Canada did not approve the use of guide lines too strongly, may I point out that its comments in this regard were contained in the third annual review published in November, 1966, almost a year ago. To condense what was said in the report I point out that, the council suggested there were a number of measures which might be adopted. It did not urge the placing of too great reliance upon an incomes policy or a guide lines policy, under normal conditions, though it made it plain that if conditions continued to worsen it might be necessary to adopt such a course. Chapter 5 of the review issued in 1966 contained a number of proposals connected with

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin monetary and fiscal policy, the possibility of using an incomes policy, and so on. A number of alternatives are indicated.
As I consider the government's actions, I do not think much has been done in the field of guide lines. I would refer hon. members to page 43 of the fourth annual review where the Economic Council had this to say-and I am sure that in making this statement the council intended it to be taken in conjunction with what had been said in the third report with regard to guide lines. I quote:
There is a clear possibility that strong underlying private demand pressures, accompanied by rapidly rising government expenditures, may exceed the capacity of the economy to accommodate them, and thus result in unacceptably high price and cost pressures over the medium-term future. This possibility is one which requires special attention in the present circumstances.
I suggest this is a direct invitation to the government to consider, among other proposals, the question of guide lines at this time. I know this presents a difficulty for hon. gentlemen opposite. I addressed a question today to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) with regard to the implementation of the proposals made by the Glassco royal commission. If my arithmetic is right, there are still almost 120 recommendations of that commission which have yet to be implemented.
The commission made its report four and a half years ago. The recommendations were in the hands of the government when it took office in 1963. I think it is a sad story when we are told after all these years that 120 of its recommendations still remain to be implemented. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to take part in the debate on the budget.
At the outset, may I say that a budget must necessarily either balance or tip over. The more we advance, the more we apply the principles of our present-day economy, the more we throw our budget out of balance. The more we grant salary increases, the more we levy taxes; the more we increase the rate of interest, the more we unbalance the budget and our economy, and the more we increase the cost of living. The more the cost of living

October 5, 1967

increases, the more the value of the dollar goes down. It is said that the value of the dollar should be brought back to par, and all the rest. When will the value of the dollar return to par, if we keep on running the administration of the country like at the present time?
Mr. Speaker, it is a pity to see and hear the Minister of Finance of Canada (Mr. Sharp) declaring in the face of Canada and the whole world his professional incompetence.
The minister admits his incapacity to deal with the present problem, although it is easy to solve. If the amendments to the Bank Act which were proposed at the previous session had been passed, the budget would now be balanced; Canada's debt would be repaid within 10 years, everybody's taxes would be reduced by 50 per cent. I can prove it. As a matter of fact, I did it before.
So, our memorable centennial year is marred by the greatest administrative failure, in the second most prosperous country of the world. Is it not said that Canada is the most prosperous country after the United States? If we are that prosperous, how is it that we are unable to balance our budget? Why are we unable to stop the rise in the cost of living and the devaluation of our dollar? Why? If war broke out tomorrow morning, the minister would find solutions to all the problems.
I would like to speak less harshly to the minister, but, as a taxpayer and a member of this house it is my duty to tell him things which I do not like to say. However, these are actual facts that must be pointed out. The world fair in Montreal simply showed, for all the world to see, the inability of our Minister of Finance to make at least a coherent speech, to provide logical explanations and to refute the illogicality of our financial situation, as reflected by increased production, continuing progressive deficits, a tremendous and fantastic capitalization, envied throughout the world but also by perpetual debts and deficits within the administration and at all levels of government. The accounts of the provincial governments, municipalities and school boards show large deficits-a really shameful situation in a country such as Canada.
The profits made by large companies are increasing, there are even cases of a capitalization of $20 billion on a $62 billion production, and yet it is impossible to balance the budget of the country. It is impossible to give
The Budget-Mr. Latulippe some encouragement to these who lack the very necessities of life and get deeper and deeper in debt because of their inadequate income.
The higher the taxes, the smaller the purchasing power of the taxpayers, who then find it increasingly difficult to make an honest living in a country overflowing with wealth.
When the government must refund $350 million worth of old debts at 3| per cent, it can find nothing better to do than to borrow the same amounts anew at 6 per cent, that is to cause a 60 per cent increase over a period of 26 years. Shame. Curses. The mind flounders. Unspeakable behaviour or misconduct on the part of a human being who bears the title of Minister of Finance.
"Let us make man in Our image, after Our likeness", said the Great Master on the first page of the Bible. It was certainly not the face of the Finance Minister of Canada which He saw then in His divine wisdom.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, God's administration shows better balance and more majesty. The sun, the moon, the stars, the earth, the rivers, the oceans, all that runs better than the words of the Minister of Finance when he mutters his undecipherable labyrinths of economic theories that seem learned because they are incomprehensible.
The minister will not stoop to the present system. He does not want to understand the simplicity of the system; he prefers to understand complexity and try to understand whatever is complex or unsoluble.
The people are aware of the failure, of the administrative failure of our governments. And I say that for the Conservatives as well as for the Liberals, because when the Conservatives were in office, they did nothing else than redeem bonds at 2, 3, 4, 4J and 5 per cent. Increasing high finance, making the rich wealthier and the poor poorer, the Conservatives did that as much as the Liberals. Whichever party, there is no difference at all. We are facing the same situation and the same problem when the government changes, the only thing that is done is to change the driver. The car is worn out and should be replaced; but instead of changing it for a new model, the driver only is replaced. Nothing more is done.
What will the new Leader of the Opposition do in the present situation with our pile of debts and deficits, with an upside down, unbalanced budget and economy? There is
October 5, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Latulippe nothing more to understand in that economy. What will he do about all those things?
It is said that a change of political party will change all that. The whole system needs changing, Mr. Speaker, and to change it the Liberals and the Conservatives must get it into their heads that they must deal with the problem. To solve it, there is no other way than grappling with it and overcoming it.
We pay $3,600,000 for a royal inquiry on taxation, we receive a 2,600 page report where it is shown that large corporations must be taxed at the same rates as individuals. But the Minister of Finance prefers to listen to the bankers, manufacturers and brokers associations as well as the chambers of commerce, which utter their unanimous objection to the conclusions of the Carter report. Should the people come and ask the minister to support and implement the decisions contained in the Carter report, he would turn his back on them and pretend not to hear. Carry on, great learned gentlemen, but remember that the Lord is watching you and that the people see you.
Deficits, unbalance, mismanagement, shame before the world, all that does not affect us any more. Our friends pile up billions, no kidding, more than $20 billion in capitalization on $62 billion in production during the year 1967. Therefore, who piles up those billions out of the people's poverty? No one else but the directors of 800 large corporations who make more than $1 million every year in declared profits.
[DOT] 15:20 p.m.)
Why such surpluses and profits on the one hand and such deficits and debts on the other? There is only one possible answer, that is the Minister of Finance is incompetent or an accomplice, clumsy or dishonest. He can choose the qualification which he prefers since he chooses the means available to balance the Canadian budget and distribute the benefits of the national economy taking into account the individuals, families and companies, the income, expenses and profits, taxes and reserves, employers, employees and private citizens, factories, shops and kitchens, capital, labour and the right of citizens who have no capital and no employment.
The Minister of Finance no longer deserves any indulgence, because he is responsible for the situation. He is responsible for everything that is done within the government because he runs the government. He is responsible for


the resulting damage and he is guilty of pursuing a fiscal policy which is leading us to final disaster, when he could prevent it.
May I have the attention of the house for one moment? Can any of the 265 members or ministers of the crown consider the following facts with unconcern?
In Montreal, workers earning $8,000 are asking for $11,000: flat refusal; strike. In Quebec city, professionals earning $32,000 are asking for $44,000. Refusal, strike. In Ottawa, capitalists making profits of $37,500 are asking for $60,000: full agreement without any discussion and automatic extension for 26 years, if you please. And that is the renewal of the loan of $225 million, that was granted over and above the other one for $235 million.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, one million dollars at 3| per cent; that is $37,500, but at 6 per cent, it represents $60,000. Therefore, our Canadian millionaires who already made $37,500 a year on each million dollars loaned to the government of the people will now get $60,000 for that same million, without doing a stitch more work.
That is where the Minister of Finance should look and see, and act by applying sanctions. Go ahead. You represent the people. The people can just as well pay $60,000 as $37,500 to its millionaires. But, who pays for elections, publicity, university professors, speech writers, perhaps even the speeches of the Minister of Finance?
If a good bus driver asks for $3,000 more, he is roundly denounced, and if a professional asks for an increase of $12,000, the outcry is somewhat smaller, but if a millionaire asks for an increase of $22,500, the Minister of Finance immediately gives in with an elegant smile and hands over the gift quietly, without anybody knowing about it. Millionaires must not be exposed to the misinterpretations of the people, their newspapermen, trade-unionists and other defenders.
If there is such disparity in the treatment of the classes of our society, the trade-unionists who make $8,000, the professionals who earn $32,000, the capitalists whose $37,500 are suddenly increased to $60,000, we should also think of the other citizens who pay unemployment insurance and earn less than $5,400 a year, not enough to pay income tax, or who do not earn any income at all but wb<' must
