nevertheless pay taxes in order to take care of the interest on the $28 billion debt which the government must pay, stuck as it is with such a Minister of Finance. Not only the present Minister of Finance but all before him have been that way. None of them has ever balanced the budget for years and years. No other solution has been found, no other means than building up masses of deficits and increasing the debt of the people and impoverishing the population, thus reducing the purchasing power of the citizens.
Do you want more follies due to our Canadian finance ministers? One thing should be recalled in this abnormal situation of our finances. We have lost control and we do not wish to take it back because we do not have it yet on our shoulders. We do not have it yet in our minds, that control of the country. But it is still time to get it back. There is still time to take it back and follow the right path. Let us aim properly and not miss the mark.
Mr. Speaker, no purpose is served by speaking any longer in the house. I am simply asking the Minister of Finance to grant me a private interview. I will meet him with pleasure. I will give him face to face the explanations. I know it would be profitable to him and that he would be satisfied just like the Canadian people.
Pending his invitation, in view of the uneasiness indicated by strikes, by inflation, by the deficits of our public administrations, in view of the increase of interest rates, the increase in workers' wages and the increase in government taxes which all contribute to the increased prices and higher cost of living even for those who have no income, no work and no capital, I would recommend that you read over the speech I made on September 9, 1966, at the time of the C.N.R. employees' strike, a strike which necessitated a special session of parliament last year. Look over also my speech of February 15, 1967, in this House of Commons on inflation of capital and deflation of purchasing power for more than half of our working population. Look over again the brief I submitted to the banking committee on October 25, 1966, which was officially delivered only on March 16, 1967 in the 53rd and last issue of the reports of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs.
These three public and official documents by themselves represent an over-all view of
DEBATES	2855
The Budget-Mr. Latulippe our economic situation, of the main uneasiness, of the major imbalance between the various elements of our national economy and simultaneously indicate efficient means to set things right rapidly without interfering with the basic structure of our monetary, economic or political institutions.
If it is recognized that the conventional and orthodox fashion of carrying out our public affairs has led Canada to a disastrous situation, as stated by the Minister of Finance it certainly proves Canada's economy must be considered anew.
Instead of always favouring the financial tycoons or the members of our powerful unions, some day or other, and the sooner the better, we will at least have to consider our economy, not in the light of capital and labour but also and above all, in the light of the needs of the many citizens who have no income, no work and no money.
The minister and the hon. members know that, in Canada, one third of our people who are able-bodied, live on social welfare at the expense of their fellow citizens. It is like robbing Peter to support Paul. And this has reached such a point that those who are working, have so many deductions from their salary that they are no better off than those on relief.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
So, Canadian people get discouraged, and this explains why there is so much dissatisfaction in Canada. As you know, raising salaries and the cost of living does not solve the problem. It is also well known that unions look out for themselves by demanding all kinds of salary increases, but this only raises the cost of living. The problem is never solved. As time goes by, things become increasingly difficult for others who do not belong to unions, who are unemployed. As you know, there are 7 million workers in Canada. Of this number, there are close to 2,400,000 people, I think, who do not earn enough money to pay income tax.
So, Mr. Speaker, the situation is more than critical. Those who pay income tax are a minority; in brief, it is always the low income workers who put money in the pockets of people in the higher brackets.
Indeed, every increase in interest rates, that is allowed benefits the big fellow at the expense of the little fellow. That is the kind of government we have, the kind we always had, because we never had any men who
2856	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Latulippe really worked for the people. We represent the financial community, of course, but we also represent the rank and file. This we should never forget, although we unfortunately have forgotten it in the past. This is the main difference between the new approach in regard to the management of our present and future economy and the old approach, the conventional and orthodox method which has put us in a most disastrous situation.
This is not the time to panic. Pretending that nothing can be done would not get us anywhere. Let us think this way: our methods have been good and efficient for many years and in much more difficult times, but today they are obsolete, out of date. They must of necessity be renewed, adapted to the new circumstances, transposed to the new economy which is obviously required.
Instead of remaining bogged down in our old thoughts, our old methods, our old customs, let us adopt a new methods of distribution which will meet the essential needs of each and every family in Canada, on the basis of our actual superabundant production, even if the yearly rate of growth of our national capitalization has to be somewhat reduced.
All our economists, engineers and advisers have long enough emphasized productivity, capitalization, financial, commercial and industrial concentration; the time has now come to balance all those achievements against the needs of people who cannot enjoy them, who cannot participate in them, simply because the methods used in the distribution of the purchasing power have remained tied to the old techniques of capital and labour, which suit only 7,400,000 citizens and ignore the 13 other millions dependent upon our total population of 20,400,000 Canadians who have the right to live.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read again at this stage a small portion of the speech made by the hon. Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp), which can be found on page 2731 of Hansard, and I quote:
I am concerned about these high Interest rates.
I regret very much that interest rates have had to rise. They have been rising throughout the western world. They have been rising in industrialized countries and in the underdeveloped countries of the world. As I said in my statement on motions today, last week I was in Rio. There, I had the

DEBATES	October 5, 1967
opportunity to meet all the ministers of finance of the world. We met many times in large groups and in small groups. One of the main problems we discussed was the problem of interest rates. As I said jokingly to one of my friends today, it was pleasant to meet with ministers of finance from around the world because at least we could console one another. We looked at this problem; we examined it carefully and at length for a week. There was not one of us who could come up with an easy or early solution to the problem of high interest rates.
But I think that the minister had forgotten to take a Creditist along.
Now then, it is impossible to argue, it is impossible to go on with a system such as that which rules the country at the moment. I said, right in the beginning, that it should either balance or tip over. Well, it is about to tip over since every step taken by the Minister of Finance is helping to make our economy tip over.
When our economy tips over, it will be hard to set it back on an even keel and I wonder if it is the present minister who will have the courage to do so.
Now, why criticize and denounce the present financial system? Because it falls short of its aim, because it does not fulfill its purpose.
The purpose of the financial system, Mr. Speaker, is to finance the production and the distribution of goods to meet the needs. When it does that, the financial system discharges its responsibility, it plays its part; otherwise, it does not play its part, it does something else, in short it is out of character.
Well, the present financial system is out of character it does not perform its function, it does not reach the goals and purposes that it should. It does not reach its objective because there are public and private goods required by the people which it would be physically possible to supply but for the financial system's inability to finance production. On the other hand, there are goods to be provided to needy persons or families who are unable to have them, because the financial system does not finance consumption. Production is inadequately financed and consumption is still less financed because the consumer is denied his purchasing power.
Each time investments and all those related matters are mentioned, it is stated that we must obtain foreign capital, because Canadians do not have the necessary capital. Why, Mr. Speaker, do Canadians not have the required capital to invest in Canada, to develop our economy? Because the Minister of
October 5, 1967

Finance is overburdening them with taxes, and afterwards, the federal, provincial and municipal governments, as well as the school boards sell bonds and get hold of the money of those who have succeeded in making some savings. There is nothing left for private enterprise, then; yet, that is where there are shortcomings in our economy. That is where they do not see that there is something to be done, that they refuse to assume their responsibilities.
There are heavy responsibilities to be assumed. It is unfortunate that there are so few members in the house because I have many things to say. I shall, however, limit myself because I have spoken enough and because the Minister of Finance knows what to do. If he does not do it, it is because he does not want to do it or because he is so well bound that he cannot budge. There is something wrong somewhere. If he is bound, well, let us free him. It is up to us to free him.
Mr. Speaker, we should have financial credit. We should be able to finance all our production, and also every citizen who benefits from social welfare allowances-at least a third of the population is either idle or unproductive-should be put to work so as to contribute to production. In spite of the fact that many of our fellow citizens live at the expense of the others, thanks to social welfare-which means that they do not produce -we managed to reach, in 1967, a total production of $62 billion. We capitalized $20 billion and also a large percentage of the income-I had it here somewhere-with a $62 billion production-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have resumed consideration of the budget debate, interrupted June 6 last and, more especially, of the motion of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) for the house to go into committee of ways and means.
After this motion, the official opposition moved an amendment which reads as follows:
That all the words after "That" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this government has failed miserably to set an example of responsibility by its refusal to reduce taxation, by its reckless increase in governmental expenditures, thus contributing to the steadily rising cost of production to the great detriment of the Canadian economy and to the sharp increase in the cost of living, already overburdensome to the Canadian people."
Furthermore, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) moved the following amendment to the amendment:
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words between the word "taxation" and the words "the sharp increase" and by substituting therefor the following words: "particularly its failure to revise the income tax structure so that a married couple with an annual income of $4,000 or less would not be subject to tax; its failure to remove the sales tax from building materials and supplies used in housing construction: and its failure to take any steps to deal with"
The end of the main amendment follows.
Yesterday, the Minister of Finance gave the house a summary of our economic situation as he sees it, followed by an outline of the revenue and expenditures and, finally, by a few remarks about the changes in the tariff rates brought about by the Kennedy round and many other matters.
The minister underlined satisfactory economic prospects with regard to employment and our balance of payments and he indicated also a strong demand in exports and consumer goods. All in all, the future was not cloudless but quite good, taking into account the increasing trend in prices and the cost of living.
The minister also told us that the most important problem was to manage our prosperity and that he did not anticipate a future
October 5, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Lachance reversal of the trend towards progress in our economy.
He implied that production was increasing at a normal rate of approximately 7 per cent and that we are succeeding fairly well in changing from the system of accelerated expansion of last year to the more reasonable rate of growth which has recently become noticeable.
I do not intend to summarize the minister's staiement, but I wish to stress his intellectual honesty and his frankness.
However, I read with anguish recently that the Vietnam war is giving rise to an international financial situation that cannot but concern us. That is why the government must unite with all other countries to try and restore peace in that part of the world.
Of course, restoring peace is not the only reason, but it is an excellent one in the framework of our present discussion.
The hon. minister endeavours to prove and suggest that the government is reducing the expenditures planned for the coming year.
I agree with this, but I favour above all the planning of priorities in expenditures. I should like to stress the importance of a few of these. I shall not give them in order of priority, but just mention them as they occur to me. To my mind, they are all important and deserve priority.
For instance, the extrapolation of Expo could be on the part of the rest of Canada, a gesture of friendliness and confidence toward the province of Quebec. There is no need to underline the outstanding success that celebration has had on the occasion of the centennial of confederation, but it is now coming to an end. Studies have been made on the future possibilities of Expo, and each and every one of us may have personal ideas on what uses it could be put to.
I feel that, in connection with reducing expenditures, priority should be given to the future of Expo, whether it is used for educational purposes-which I would favour-or touristic or any other purpose.
I trust the federal government, as it has done in the past for that demonstration, will continue to give its whole-hearted support.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, priority should also be given to reform of our penal institutions and our judiciary system in Canada, so that we might solve rapidly the problem of rehabilitation of those who must pay their debt to society.

I have had the opportunity of discussing this matter several times in the house; it is one of my favourite topics.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Although the matter has been tossed around for a few years, I must say I still do not see being taken by the government in this area, legislative action of the kind that would provide for the suppression of criminal records, for instance, or the development of a rehabilitation agency for ex-convicts that would promote planned training in our penitentiaries and see that all civil service doors, be they federal, provincial or municipal, are eventually open to released convicts; in short, a humane penal reform that goes beyond prison stone walls.
There is another priority matter which could, I hope, avoid the steam-roller; I mean the field of education and manpower retraining.

I said amongst other things:
The evolution of the human race and the new needs created by scientific progress require us to reassess our teaching methods and adapt them to the new needs. Personally, I am just as much in favour of eventual constitutional reforms to meet the new needs and the legitimate aspirations of the new generation.
Some are against too drastic constitutional changes and prefer a slow but progressive evolution; others are more in favour of a special status for all the provinces, which some are loudly requesting at least for the province of Quebec.
Personally, I believe that a careful study of the present political situation, of our constitutional documents and of our present and future needs will show the necessity of making some major changes both in the spirit and in the letter of our Canadian constitution.
After a hundred years, it is undeniable that the province of Quebec has become the fatherland of French Canadians and that, on that basis, it must give to all its French-speaking citizens the best possible means of subsistence and development, without forgetting, nevertheless, that other Frenchspeaking Canadians are scattered throughout Canada-
But after a hundred years, it is undeniable that it would be in the interest of the provincial and federal governments to reappraise and amend certain powers deriving from their respective jurisdiction to meet the economic and cultural needs of Canadians.
In short, it could be in the interest of the provinces to surrender to the central government, partly or entirely, temporarily or permanently, certain powers deriving from their exclusive jurisdiction and the same could apply to the central government with respect to the provinces.
And that is why, Mr. Speaker, I stressed as a priority problem federal-provincial relations with regard to the transfer of fiscal jurisdiction or of some jurisdiction, in part or in full, temporarily or permanently. I take, for instance, the problem of securities, of the various securities commissions. A hundred years ago, that sector of our economy was almost non-existent, and today, the exchange of securities is of capital importance.
The matter comes under provincial jurisdiction but, in my opinion, it should at least be under national jurisdiction or be considered on a national, if not federal, basis.
That is one example to prove how antiquated our constitution is and how much it needs to be amended, although that does not mean it must be completely changed from A to Z.

Mr. Speaker, at this stage in the budget debate I am quite sure that you and all members of the house would agree that the core of our discussion is and must be the problem of inflation, the constant increase in the cost of living, the constant erosion of the standard of living of Canadians which follows from that increase in the cost of living and inflation, and therefore the question of what to do about this problem. What can we do in the House of Commons and what can the government, which is responsible to the House of Commons, be expected and asked to do about these problems?
It is in this spirit that I should like to approach these problems; a spirit that does not minimize their seriousness, that does not minimize the difficulty of dealing with them but, on the other hand, does not excuse the government for its failures to deal with them. In this approach we, on our side, do not go so far as to say that the government can provide all the answers and solve all the problems; nor do we go so far as to say that the government is entirely responsible for the situation which now presses so heavily on the Canadian people. Notwithstanding that approach, however, we do say, and I think it is the responsibility of this House of Commons to say this to the government, that the government should take a hard look at its own position and its own conduct to see the extent to which it has contributed to the problem. It should also take a hard look at its own position in order that it may come up with answers and courses which would lead it to refrain from actions that create or aggravate the trend toward inflation.
Second, we say that not only should the government take this hard look at its own position and its own responsibility but it should take the initiative and show leadership in suggesting and following up solutions to these problems. While we are, therefore, prepared to recognize the over-all importance and over-all necessity for co-operation in the search for solutions, we say that the government must accept its primary responsibility

in the two fields I have referred to, namely, its own action in contributing to the situation and its own responsibility for suggesting solutions.
Looked at in this light I must say that the minister's speech of yesterday, his second budget resume, his second rehearsal of the fiscal policies of the government, represents a serious disappointment on both the counts that I have mentioned. That is so, because, first, the minister failed to recognize and admit that government conduct has directly contributed to the forces of inflation, has directly fanned the fires of inflation; and second, because his speech failed entirely to suggest any effective remedies for the situation that the government was prepared to apply. In this context his speech amounted to nothing more than a moral exhortation, coupled with a threat, to others to do better than the minister and the government are prepared to do themselves. There was the threat that if they do not do better, "then we are to freeze the economy and create a large measure of unemployment."
It amounted to nothing more than a moral exhortation and threat which are the more unacceptable in that the government itself shows no readiness to adopt the prudent measures and restraints that it so piously suggests and urges on others.
Let me document my case, Mr. Speaker. I have said that the government is responsible, first, because it adopts and follows policies which fan the fires of inflation. I should like to give some concrete proof of what I have said. The government does this by its direct actions as well as by the example, the bad example, that it sets to industry, labour, and >
ther parts of the Canadian economy, e (8:10 p.m.)
As my first example, I draw attention to the imposition and retention of sales tax on building materials and production equipment. We on this side recognize that the government is bound to raise revenues with which to meet its proper responsibilities and that it must therefore impose taxes. But why choose a tax which is directly inflationary in its effects? This is what the country has been asking for months. Why impose a tax which must by its very nature contribute to increases in the cost of things which are bought and sold in Canada as well as in the cost of houses which are bought, rented and lived in by Canadians? There are other sources of revenue which are not so directly inflationary; indeed the use of these sources might
October 5, 1967

well have a contrary effect. The government adopted this tax because it was not prepared to be square and fair with the Canadian people. It thought it could conceal its actions by collecting indirectly what it was not prepared to collect directly. It therefore resorted to the most reprehensible and inflationary tax it could possibly conceive.
Second in the category of actions which have fanned the fires of inflation and set a bad example to others concerned with the management of business and economic affairs, I would cite the upward spiral of government spending and extravagance. For at least three years the government has been following a trend which can only be characterized as the proliferation of its departments and staffs in the most profligate manner. This proliferation produces no results in terms of increased productivity but it does produce important and damaging results in terms of unproductive spending.
I know the minister tells this house and the press and television audiences that he is slashing expenditures, applying the axe to the level of government spending and saving money. That is the impression he tries to give. Mr. Speaker, it is a joke. In the context of the seriousness of the situation I would say, even, that it is an attempt at a hoax on the Canadian people because it has become perfectly clear during the last two days, if it were not so before, that it is not with respect to current spending that the minister is applying the axe, but with respect to next year's spending proposals.
We all know that this review of future expenditure is an annual process. Every government reviews the estimates before they are presented to the house and suggests or insists to the departments, that spending proposals be reduced. That is why the Treasury Board exists. I am disappointed, if not surprised, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) should elevate to the stature of a virtue something which is no more than his plain and simple duty.
The question is: what, if anything, has this minister done to reduce spending this year?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would be interested to hear the hon. member answer his own question because I hope his answer will indicate the concern which the Canadian people expect him to show.
When the minister asks for our approval because he is planning to reduce the spending
The Budget-Mr. Fulton proposals which the departments have submitted for next year he reminds me of the man who says: I have just saved $10,000 because though I originally proposed to buy a Rolls Royce next year I have decided to buy a Ford instead. This is the measure of the minister's boasts about the savings he will effect next year.
The Minister of Finance should be cutting down expenditures this year. Instead, he is doing the opposite, and the government of which he is a member has been doing precisely the opposite by causing a proliferation of government departments and embarking on unnecessary and extravagant spending. It seems to me that every time hon. gentlemen opposite have a new idea they set up a new department. What the country would like to see is some co-ordination instead of all this proliferation.
Let me cite particular examples. I have in mind the Department of Industry and the three departments which are now doing the job formerly done by the Department of Justice. There are other examples I could give, including the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Department of Labour and the relationship between them. However, I will deal with the examples I mentioned first as being prime examples of the point I am making.
Everything that is being done by the Department of Industry could well be done by a branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. This parliament was told when the Department of Industry was set up that it would be taking over not only personnel from the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Defence Production but that it would be carrying out functions which would otherwise fall to those two departments. It was explained that there would, therefore, be no increase in government spending but, rather, a degree of economy through increased efficiency resulting from the setting up of the new department.
Let us now examine the record in terms of personnel only-I am talking, now, only of departmental administration. One might have thought that if the Department of Industry were to take over the functions and personnel of other departments the spending of those other departments would have been reduced. Exactly the opposite has occurred. If hon. members look at the records in the blue books of estimates for the years concerned they will find that in 1963-64 when the Department of Industry was first set up it had an establishment of 274. In the estimates for

October 5. 1967
The Budget-Mr. Fulton 1967-68, the current estimates, the proposed establishment under departmental administration amounts to 783, an increase of 509, or nearly 200 per cent.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
One might be inclined to say, if the personnel in other departments had gone down, this may be a justifiable measure. But unfortunately one finds that the absolutely opposite trend has taken place. In the same narrow category, departmental administration, you find Defence Production departmental administration personnel have increased from a total of 1,699 in the year 1963-64 to 3,684 in 1967-68, an increase of 1,985, or over 100 per cent.
Let us look also at the Department of Trade and Commerce. I can appreciate that trade involves external relations, but commerce I would have thought involved domestic problems, including domestic industry. Even the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) would agree that that is a reasonable assumption.

Personnel under departmental administration in the Department of Trade and Commerce in the same year, 1963-64, the year the Department of Industry was set up, totalled 514. That is increased this year to 812. In summary, one finds that Department of Industry personnel in that category have increased by some 200 per cent, and that the other departments' personnel have increased by over 100 per cent in the one case, and by about 60 per cent in the other. So, the total

personnel involved as between the three departments, in departmental administration alone, has increased from 2,487 in the year when the Department of Industry was set up, to 5,279 in the current year's estimates, an increase of 2,792, or again over a 100 per cent increase.
If one looks at the spending figures for the Department of Industry alone, the department which we were told was going to coordinate activities, be efficient and not involve the country in greater extravagances, one finds that in the year 1964-65, the first year it really got under way, the figure given for its total spending was $25 million. In the next year, 1965-66, it was $36 million. In 1966-67 it was $51 million, and in the current year the estimated spending is $146 million, an increase of over five times, nearly six times, over the spending in the first year of the organization of that department.
One finds the same situation with respect to the division of the functions performed by the Department of Justice. Previously the Department of Justice in general terms, carried out responsibilities now assigned to three ministers, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau), the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell), and the Registrar General (Mr. Turner).
Again if one looks at the record of personnel one finds the same trend. In the year immediately prior to the division of functions the Department of Justice had a total of 220 persons engaged in departmental administration. In the year following the division, 1966-67, according to the estimates for that year Department of Justice administration personnel went up to 245, the Registrar General had 82 in that category, and the Solicitor General with a modest beginning had seven. But in this year's estimates the Department of Justice total has gone up to 341, the Registrar General has 84 and the Solicitor General 28, so that from a beginning of 220 in 1965-66, when all these functions were performed by one department, we have at the present time 453 people engaged in departmental administration, again an increase of over 100 per cent.
This is the trend to which I refer when I say that the minister and his government have been following courses which directly contribute to inflation and completely disentitle the government to make these pious, moral exhortations to business and labour in Canada with respect to the courses they should be following.
The second area of disappointment, and therefore of justifiable criticism with respect
October 5, 1967

to the minister's speech and his omission to put forward a program, is the complete failure to suggest priorities, not only within the federal government program but also failure at any attempt to get agreement with the provinces with respect to priorities to be followed in the realm of government spending and government activity generally.
I say, sir, that the minister's whole approach is wrong. I refer, for instance, to his statement on Monday of this week that with respect to priorities it is not what you put at the top but what you drop off at the bottom which counts. This is a completely impossible approach, impossible in the sense of producing any realistic results because priorities require planning, and when you make a plan you don't ask first, "What is least important for me to do?" Rather, if your plan is to have realism you ask, "What is most important for me to do?"
I know that such planning takes not only courage but judgment. I do not accuse the minister of any lack of courage but I do accuse him of complete lack of judgment in this kind of approach to the problem of priorities and planning. His attitude, of course, is the reverse of positive-that we do not discuss first what is most important to do but rather we try to decide what is least important to do; and this is the typical attitude of the Liberal party-backing into the second century of Canada's history; in other words government in reverse.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have never found that these side or snide remarks of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) are of a kind that really make much impression on anybody.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Never snide, but always constructive.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have three serious problems which I think all Canadians recognize. The first is the problem of world peace. I cannot let this opportunity pass without complimenting my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), for his recent speech at the United Nations general assembly.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On that occasion I think he said the things that are in the hearts and minds of all of us. We all know that no defence is really effective any more in this world except peace. If we kid ourselves that anything else will be effective, we are very foolish indeed.
We have a second problem that is perhaps closer to us here and we are very much aware of it. That is the question of the continuation of confederation and the unity of our country.
I am not at all convinced that it is helpful for people like myself from English speaking Canada to say too much about this question at the present time. I think we all have a sympathy and understanding of the difficulties through which our friends and colleagues from Quebec have been going. I think we have a much better appreciation now of some of the injustices from which our friends from Quebec have suffered. I think those of us who are not French speaking are fully determined that if we have the chance we want to rectify those injustices. But I believe we know that primarily these things must be settled and determined by our friends from the province of Quebec, and that the rest of us should be cautious, careful and moderate in our language.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
2866	COMMONS

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There may not be the same unanimity on the next question, but I think the great majority of Canadians feel that there is a third problem.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Liberal government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us not be silly.
Not only have we the problem of obtaining peace in the world in which we live, not only have we the problem of achieving unity within our country, but we also have the problem, living next door to the greatest nation in the world, of maintaining our own independence. Most of us in one way or another are searching for the solution to that problem. I hope that before very many months have passed, the government will be able to table a white paper which will at least provide a focus for debate about what should be done in this respect.
Apart from those three problems, if we are honest and fair, and if we really lift up our heads and think ahead, we must agree that this is the country with the greatest future of any country in the world.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have a tremendous potential and a terrific opportunity. If we indulge in too much petty squabbling over little problems, I think we will perhaps forget the real opportunities that we have. Those are some of the reasons, Mr. Speaker, for my mild disappointment in the speech of my hon. friend, for whom I have the greatest admiration. I think he exaggerated our present economic difficulties out of all perspective.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I expected you to say that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

But I wonder whether my hon. friend has informed himself of the projections of most of the best analysts in this country, who suggest that the inflationary pressures that were obvious and evident in 1966 and the beginning of this year are clearly moderating, and that the expectations for

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Anyway, Mr. Speaker, with the greatest respect, I do not think my hon. friend has contributed very much this evening either to the knowledge or the peace of mind of the people of this country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why not?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not the real cause of the increase in the cost of housing. Nobody in this country who has any sense of responsibility is unaware of or unconcerned about the increased cost of housing. But I suggest to all hon. members that most of us have taken a little trouble to analyse the real reasons for this increase in cost. We all know, if we have done that, that most of the increase, or the biggest single increase in the cost of a home results from the increased cost of land.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ah.

speechtext:
It seems to me that although my hon. friend was perhaps trying to be helpful, his efforts were not too impressive, even given the scope of the problems to which he was addressing himself. He suggested that one of our great troubles was caused by the separation of the Departments of Trade and Commerce and of Industry. In a happier era when I was self employed I happened to be engaged in the business of management consulting and I was fully aware of the principles of organization. One of the principles of organization which I would commend to my hon. friend is that one does not combine two dissimilar functions under one head. The main objective of the Department of Trade and Commerce is to promote exports. The main objective of the Department of Industry is to promote the manufacturing industry; not all industry, not farming, not wheat growing, not the production of pulp and paper and our other great export industries, but to concentrate primarily, although not entirely, on the manufacturing sector. Before the Department of Industry

The Budget-Mr. Gordon was created, manufacturing in this country was no one's prime responsibility. This may not have mattered very much to my hon. friend for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) but it mattered a great deal to industry and to the people employed in industry, both in the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario. One of the things which we thought was important was to have a minister who, first of all, would be informed about the problems of the manufacturing industry and, second, would proceed to do something about them. Everyone knows that the sector which is developing at the fastest rate in our export trade is manufacturing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thought the Department of Trade and Commerce was interested in exports.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Of course it is, but you cannot export things until you have them produced at prices which can compete in world markets. Perhaps my hon. friend may not know this but I suspect there are members on his side of the house who are not completely unfamiliar with the manufacturing sector or the millions of people who find their employment in the manufacturing industry. This is something which will be increasingly important in the future and, whether we like it or not, I think it is desirable. I, for one, think we need a minister and a department concentrating on that matter.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We certainly do.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Did I hear a voice from the wilderness? I have great respect for the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald) and I will not comment on what he said except to say that he has to do better than that.
The hon. member for Kamloops stated that we must establish priorities. Everyone agrees with that. However, we all know that the priorities upon which some of us might agree may not be too acceptable to others. It so happens there is a difference in political philosophies.
For example I was surprised that my hon. friend should have raised doubts about the importance of medicare in Canada. There are no doubts on this subject on this side of the house. We in the Liberal party are for medicare. We are committed to it and we will do our damndest to see that it is implemented. It may be that some Conservative elements opposite would prefer to see this great improvement in social security dropped, deferred, or put off.

speechtext: I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I was surprised to hear a man who very nearly won the leadership of the great party opposite suggest in this house that this particular social measure should be put aside. If that is my hon. friend's idea of priorities, we want no part of it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure that my hon. friend would not wish to deliberately distort what I said. I said that I felt the Minister of Finance should discuss with the provinces not only the date of implementation of the medicare plan but some of the aspects of the medicare program which the federal government has imposed on them. Is the minister opposed to discussing with the provinces a program in which they have a very real interest?

I apologize to the hon. member if even by inference I appeared to distort anything he might have said. I would remind him, however, that a law has been passed by this parliament and so far as I am concerned, and I am sure so far as most hon. members are concerned, this law should be implemented.
I did not mean to enter into a heated debate when I rose to speak. I only wished to emphasize that in my opinion this country is not in the dire straits which my hon. friend seemed to suggest. 1 think we are on the threshold of a tremendous improvement in the standard of living of all Canadians. I suggest to hon. members who take a different view that in the last five years-I will not say in the last four years so as not to be accused of inadvertent partisanship-
